kernels.definition: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that comes in positive and negative forms and determines electric interactions.

definitionAnchor.quote: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter.

facts.text: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

anchor.quote: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

facts.text: Net charge is conserved in an isolated system.

kernels.definition: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.

definitionAnchor.quote: The electric field is the electric force per unit charge.

facts.text: The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.

anchor.quote: the direction of the force on a positive test charge

facts.text: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

anchor.quote: closer field lines indicate a stronger field

kernels.definition: Gauss's law relates the net electric flux through a closed surface to the net charge enclosed by that surface.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge

facts.text: A Gaussian surface is useful for calculating fields when symmetry makes the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface.

anchor.quote: Use symmetry to determine the electric field

facts.text: Zero enclosed charge implies zero net flux, not necessarily zero electric field everywhere on the surface.

anchor.quote: the net flux depends only on the charge enclosed

kernels.definition: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge; potential difference is the work per unit charge required to move between two points.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric potential energy per unit charge

facts.text: Only potential differences affect work and energy changes in electrostatics.

anchor.quote: only differences in potential energy are physically meaningful

facts.text: Electric field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential.

anchor.quote: electric field points in the direction of decreasing potential

kernels.definition: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.

definitionAnchor.quote: capacitance is the amount of charge stored per volt

facts.text: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors.
For a parallel-plate capacitor, increasing plate area increases capacitance and increasing separation decreases capacitance.

anchor.quote: capacitance is directly proportional to the area and inversely proportional to the separation

kernels.definition: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric current is the rate at which charge flows

facts.text: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.
Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

anchor.quote: constant velocity, known as the drift velocity

mcItems.q: Two identical plastic balls are given the same kind of charge and then brought near each other. What happens when they are close together?
op: They push apart because like charges repel.
They pull together because like charges attract.
They do neither because charge has no effect on matter.
They always become neutral when they are close together.
mcItems.ex: They push apart because like charges repel. A common mistake is to think identical charges draw together, but the stated interaction is repulsion for like charges and attraction for unlike charges.

mcItems.q: A charged object is placed in an isolated system and no charge is added or removed. Which statement best matches the situation?
op: The net charge stays the same.
The net charge disappears.
The net charge becomes positive.
The net charge changes whenever the object moves.
mcItems.ex: The net charge stays the same. A likely misconception is that motion alone changes charge, but the conserved quantity in an isolated system is net charge, not position or movement.

keyTerms.df: A property of matter that remains available in equal total amount within an isolated system.
keyTerms.eg: When an isolated setup is watched from start to finish, the total net charge is not created or destroyed.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the object’s temperature.
keyTerms.cx: Total charge is conserved in an isolated system.

keyTerms.df: Two charges with the same sign, which interact by pushing apart.
keyTerms.eg: Two positively charged tape pieces move away from each other when brought close.
keyTerms.mi: They always cancel each other out.
keyTerms.cx: Same-sign charges repel; opposite-sign charges attract.

mcItems.q: Which statement best matches the meaning of electric field at a point in space?
op: The force on a positive test charge divided by the charge amount at that point
The total force on every nearby charge added together
The potential energy stored by a charge at that point
The number of field lines crossing a surface at that point
mcItems.ex: It is the force per unit positive test charge, so dividing force by charge gives the field. A common confusion is to treat the field as the force itself, but the force depends on how much charge the test object has.

mcItems.q: What does the direction of an electric field tell you?
op: The way a positive test charge would accelerate
The way a negative test charge would accelerate
Where the field is strongest everywhere
How much charge is moving through the region
mcItems.ex: The field points in the direction a positive test charge would accelerate, so that is the correct choice. A tempting mistake is to reverse the direction because negative charges respond oppositely, but the stated direction is defined using a positive test charge.

keyTerms.df: A vector quantity that gives the electric force per unit positive test charge at a point.
keyTerms.eg: At one location in a lab setup, the field is described by how much force a tiny positive test charge would feel there.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as the charge on the object placed in the region.
keyTerms.cx: The charge placed in the region can be different from the field, which is defined by force per unit positive test charge.

keyTerms.df: How crowded the field lines appear in a diagram, indicating relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: In a sketch of two regions, the denser cluster of lines marks the place with stronger field.
keyTerms.mi: More lines always mean more total charge is present.
keyTerms.cx: Line crowding in a picture shows relative field strength, not the amount of charge by itself.

mcItems.q: A closed surface encloses no net charge. What does Gauss's law say about the net electric flux through that surface?
op: The net flux must be zero.
The electric field must be zero everywhere on the surface.
The flux depends only on the surface's area.
The enclosed charge must be negative.
mcItems.ex: The net flux must be zero because zero enclosed charge implies zero net flux through the closed surface. A common mistake is to treat zero flux as meaning the electric field is zero everywhere, but the field may still be present on the surface.

mcItems.q: Why is a Gaussian surface especially useful in some charge problems?
op: It can make the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface when symmetry is favorable.
It always gives the electric field directly from the flux.
It works only when the enclosed charge is zero.
It measures potential energy without using charge.
mcItems.ex: It can make the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface when symmetry is favorable. The misconception is that the surface itself somehow creates the field result, but the usefulness comes from symmetry making the field easier to handle.

keyTerms.df: A chosen closed surface used to take advantage of symmetry in field calculations.
keyTerms.eg: A spherical surface around a point charge is a Gaussian surface because the symmetry makes the field easier to relate to the surface.
keyTerms.mi: It is a physical shell that changes the charge distribution inside it.
keyTerms.cx: A Gaussian surface is a mathematical choice, not a material object, and it is picked to match symmetry.

keyTerms.df: The total electric flow through a closed surface, linked to how much charge the surface encloses.
keyTerms.eg: If a closed surface encloses no net charge, the net electric flux through it is zero.
keyTerms.mi: It is the electric field strength at one point on the surface.
keyTerms.cx: Flux summarizes the whole closed surface, while field strength describes the field at a location.

mcItems.q: A student compares two points in an electrostatic setup. Which statement best describes what determines the work needed to move a charge from one point to the other?
op: the potential difference between the two points
the electric field at one point
the charge's potential energy alone
the path length through the region
mcItems.ex: The work per unit charge is set by the potential difference between the two points. A single-point field value, the charge's potential energy by itself, and the path length do not by themselves state the energy change described here.

mcItems.q: If electric potential is higher on the left than on the right, which way does the electric field point?
op: from left to right
from right to left
upward
it has no direction
mcItems.ex: The electric field points toward lower electric potential, so it points from left to right in this situation. The opposite direction would go toward higher potential, which contradicts the stated relation.

keyTerms.df: Energy assigned to each unit charge at a location.
keyTerms.eg: A reading of 12 volts means each coulomb there corresponds to 12 joules of electric potential energy relative to the chosen reference.
keyTerms.mi: It is the total energy carried by the object itself.
keyTerms.cx: In a charge-and-potential activity, students compare locations by energy per unit charge rather than by the object's whole energy.

keyTerms.df: The work required for each unit charge to move between two points.
keyTerms.eg: Moving a small test charge from one plate region to another can require 5 joules per coulomb, which is a potential difference of 5 volts.
keyTerms.mi: It is the separate force on a charge at one point.
keyTerms.cx: In circuit and field questions, students use the change between two positions to predict work and energy changes.

mcItems.q: Which statement best defines capacitance for a conductor or capacitor?
op: Stored charge divided by potential difference
Potential difference divided by stored charge
Electric field strength between conductors
Energy stored divided by plate separation
mcItems.ex: Stored charge divided by potential difference is the definition of capacitance. The other choices mix up capacitance with field strength, energy, or the inverse ratio of the definition.

mcItems.q: For a parallel-plate capacitor, which change increases capacitance?
op: Larger plate area
Greater plate separation
Higher potential difference
More stored charge
mcItems.ex: Larger plate area increases capacitance for a parallel-plate capacitor. keyTerms.eg: A capacitor holding more charge at the same voltage has a larger capacitance.

keyTerms.cx: The corrected idea is that capacitance compares charge with potential difference; it is not just the charge alone.

mcItems.q: Which statement matches electric current in this workshop?
op: Charge passes through a surface at a certain rate.
Charge stored on a surface determines the circuit layout.
A surface forces charge to move rapidly through a wire.
The direction of charge motion always matches the electric signal.
mcItems.ex: Charge passing through a surface per unit time is electric current. A common mix-up is to treat current as stored charge or as the signal speed, but those are different ideas.

mcItems.q: In the conventional-current convention, which direction is used?
op: The direction positive charge would move.
The direction negative charge would move.
The direction the electric signal travels.
The direction charge is stored on the surface.
mcItems.ex: Conventional current points the way positive charge would move. A tempting mistake is to confuse that with signal speed or with an unspecified charge motion, but the convention is defined by positive charge.

keyTerms.df: Charge flow measured by how much charge crosses a surface in a given time.
keyTerms.eg: If more charge crosses a cross-section of a wire each second, the current is larger.
keyTerms.mi: Current is the same thing as the amount of charge sitting in one place.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is to focus on flow rate, not stored charge.

keyTerms.df: The direction assigned to current by imagining positive charge moving.
keyTerms.eg: When analyzing a circuit, the arrow for current is drawn in the direction a positive charge would travel.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current must point the same way every charged particle actually drifts.
keyTerms.cx: The convention follows positive-charge motion, regardless of any other microscopic details.

mcItems.q: Two identical plastic balls are given the same kind of charge and then brought near each other. What happens when they are close together?
op: They push apart because like charges repel.
They pull together because like charges attract.
They do neither because charge has no effect on matter.
They always become neutral when they are close together.
mcItems.ex: They push apart because like charges repel. A common mistake is to think identical charges draw together, but the stated interaction is repulsion for like charges and attraction for unlike charges.

mcItems.q: A charged object is placed in an isolated system and no charge is added or removed. Which statement best matches the situation?
op: The net charge stays the same.
The net charge disappears.
The net charge becomes positive.
The net charge changes whenever the object moves.
mcItems.ex: The net charge stays the same. A likely misconception is that motion alone changes charge, but the conserved quantity in an isolated system is net charge, not position or movement.

keyTerms.df: A property of matter that remains available in equal total amount within an isolated system.
keyTerms.eg: When an isolated setup is watched from start to finish, the total net charge is not created or destroyed.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the object’s temperature.
keyTerms.cx: Total charge is conserved in an isolated system.

keyTerms.df: Two charges with the same sign, which interact by pushing apart.
keyTerms.eg: Two positively charged tape pieces move away from each other when brought close.
keyTerms.mi: They always cancel each other out.
keyTerms.cx: Same-sign charges repel; opposite-sign charges attract.

mcItems.q: Which statement best matches the meaning of electric field at a point in space?
op: The force on a positive test charge divided by the charge amount at that point
The total force on every nearby charge added together
The potential energy stored by a charge at that point
The number of field lines crossing a surface at that point
mcItems.ex: It is the force per unit positive test charge, so dividing force by charge gives the field. A common confusion is to treat the field as the force itself, but the force depends on how much charge the test object has.

mcItems.q: What does the direction of an electric field tell you?
op: The way a positive test charge would accelerate
The way a negative test charge would accelerate
Where the field is strongest everywhere
How much charge is moving through the region
mcItems.ex: The field points in the direction a positive test charge would accelerate, so that is the correct choice. A tempting mistake is to reverse the direction because negative charges respond oppositely, but the stated direction is defined using a positive test charge.

keyTerms.df: A vector quantity that gives the electric force per unit positive test charge at a point.
keyTerms.eg: At one location in a lab setup, the field is described by how much force a tiny positive test charge would feel there.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same thing as the charge on the object placed in the region.
keyTerms.cx: The charge placed in the region can be different from the field, which is defined by force per unit positive test charge.

keyTerms.df: How crowded the field lines appear in a diagram, indicating relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: In a sketch of two regions, the denser cluster of lines marks the place with stronger field.
keyTerms.mi: More lines always mean more total charge is present.
keyTerms.cx: Line crowding in a picture shows relative field strength, not the amount of charge by itself.

mcItems.q: A closed surface encloses no net charge. What does Gauss's law say about the net electric flux through that surface?
op: The net flux must be zero.
The electric field must be zero everywhere on the surface.
The flux depends only on the surface's area.
The enclosed charge must be negative.
mcItems.ex: The net flux must be zero because zero enclosed charge implies zero net flux through the closed surface. A common mistake is to treat zero flux as meaning the electric field is zero everywhere, but the field may still be present on the surface.

keyTerms.df: A chosen closed surface used to take advantage of symmetry in field calculations.
keyTerms.eg: A spherical surface around a point charge is a Gaussian surface because the symmetry makes the field easier to relate to the surface.
keyTerms.mi: It is a physical shell that changes the charge distribution inside it.
keyTerms.cx: A Gaussian surface is a mathematical choice, not a material object, and it is picked to match symmetry.

keyTerms.df: The total electric flow through a closed surface, linked to how much charge the surface encloses.
keyTerms.eg: If a closed surface encloses no net charge, the net electric flux through it is zero.
keyTerms.mi: It is the electric field strength at one point on the surface.
keyTerms.cx: Flux summarizes the whole closed surface, while field strength describes the field at a location.

mcItems.q: A student compares two points in an electrostatic setup. Which statement best describes what determines the work needed to move a charge from one point to the other?
op: the potential difference between the two points
the electric field at one point
the charge's potential energy alone
the path length through the region
mcItems.ex: The work per unit charge is set by the potential difference between the two points. A single-point field value, the charge's potential energy by itself, and the path length do not by themselves state the energy change described here.

mcItems.q: If electric potential is higher on the left than on the right, which way does the electric field point?
op: from left to right
from right to left
upward
it has no direction
mcItems.ex: The electric field points toward lower electric potential, so it points from left to right in this situation. The opposite direction would go toward higher potential, which contradicts the stated relation.

keyTerms.df: Energy assigned to each unit charge at a location.
keyTerms.eg: A reading of 12 volts means each coulomb there corresponds to 12 joules of electric potential energy relative to the chosen reference.
keyTerms.mi: It is the total energy carried by the object itself.
keyTerms.cx: In a charge-and-potential activity, students compare locations by energy per unit charge rather than by the object's whole energy.

keyTerms.df: The work required for each unit charge to move between two points.
keyTerms.eg: Moving a small test charge from one plate region to another can require 5 joules per coulomb, which is a potential difference of 5 volts.
keyTerms.mi: It is the separate force on a charge at one point.
keyTerms.cx: In circuit and field questions, students use the change between two positions to predict work and energy changes.

keyTerms.eg: A capacitor holding more charge at the same voltage has a larger capacitance.
keyTerms.mi: Capacitance is the amount of charge a device must always contain.
keyTerms.cx: The corrected idea is that capacitance compares charge with potential difference; it is not just the charge alone.

keyTerms.df: A capacitor made from two conducting plates whose geometry controls how easily charge is stored.

keyTerms.cx: The geometry matters in opposite ways: more area raises capacitance, but more separation lowers it.

mcItems.q: Which statement matches electric current in this workshop?
op: Charge passes through a surface at a certain rate.
Charge stored on a surface determines the circuit layout.
A surface forces charge to move rapidly through a wire.
The direction of charge motion always matches the electric signal.
mcItems.ex: Charge passing through a surface per unit time is electric current. A common mix-up is to treat current as stored charge or as the signal speed, but those are different ideas.

mcItems.q: In the conventional-current convention, which direction is used?
op: The direction positive charge would move.
The direction negative charge would move.
The direction the electric signal travels.
The direction charge is stored on the surface.
mcItems.ex: Conventional current points the way positive charge would move. A tempting mistake is to confuse that with signal speed or with an unspecified charge motion, but the convention is defined by positive charge.

keyTerms.df: Charge flow measured by how much charge crosses a surface in a given time.
keyTerms.eg: If more charge crosses a cross-section of a wire each second, the current is larger.
keyTerms.mi: Current is the same thing as the amount of charge sitting in one place.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is to focus on flow rate, not stored charge.

keyTerms.df: The direction assigned to current by imagining positive charge moving.
keyTerms.eg: When analyzing a circuit, the arrow for current is drawn in the direction a positive charge would travel.
keyTerms.mi: Conventional current must point the same way every charged particle actually drifts.
keyTerms.cx: The convention follows positive-charge motion, regardless of any other microscopic details.
